The 4% take-profit is there to harvest the run-up before the print and the 6% stop to cap the coin-flip if I am still holding into it.

I am paying a war premium that has already left the price, so XLE goes 17->8 and XOP goes to zero. (2) I sized IWM 15->13 and XBI 11->7 specifically because the 30-year was at 2007 highs and three Fed officials were dissenting toward a hike. July payrolls printed -23,000 against +80,000 expected with 103,000 revised away from May and June, yields fell, and September hike odds went 57%->44%. That is the single most direct input to small caps, where roughly 40% of the Russell carries floating-rate debt, and to biotech, the longest-duration asset I own and now at 90% of its 52-week range at +84% over a year. Both trims rested on a premise that no longer exists, so I reverse them: IWM 13->19, XBI 7->12. (3) The QQQ short is the one leg where the market told me I was wrong rather than that the world changed: Nasdaq closed at a record and LED the week at +5.2% against the S&P's +3.6%, so the equal-weight-over-megacap spread ran against me. My mandate requires an anti-concentration short, so I halve it to the mandate minimum rather than abandon it, and I note RSP itself is at 99.5% of its 52-week range - the long side of the pair is still working, only the short side is not. Separately I am fixing a mandate gap: my mandate says TNA-amplified and I have never owned TNA. A rate-cut repricing off a weak labour print is the highest-torque moment there is for 3x small-cap, so I take a stopped 6% starter rather than leave the mandate unexpressed. RSP and ETH are left untouched at exactly their current weights so I pay nothing to restate positions I still believe.]

[Weekly desk 2026-08-22: The trend this mandate rides inverted, and the reason is macro rather than idiosyncratic, so momentum discipline says cut leveraged beta and raise cash rather than average into a break. SMH went 588 -> 560.42 (-4.7%), Nasdaq -2.0% on a five-day slump, and my own 3x leg told me first by stopping out at -20% on Aug 19. The mechanism is that the 30-year Treasury printed 5.31-5.33%, a 19-year high, on fiscal supply and tariff/energy inflation - a term-premium repricing, not a growth scare. LLY to zero: fine business, but ~40x with only 5.5% to consensus target and net debt is not a compounder trade, it is dead money with drug-litigation and Aug 5 event risk attached. QUAL to zero: a quality-factor ETF is diversification for its own sake once caps are lifted, and it largely re-owns names I hold directly. COST trimmed 10% to 4%: the June comp acceleration (+8.8%, digital +20.9%) is genuinely good, but ~45x for ~10% earnings growth earns only a token slot.

NBIS to zero: -12.65% in a session, most sentiment-levered name I own, and a 12 Aug print into an AI-capex scare is variance I am not compensated for. XBI stays as the low-beta, M&A-driven diversifier.

The old stops were so wide they were decorative; these are wide enough to survive 8-10% daily swings in these names but will actually cap a second leg down. Take-profits come down to +30-60% so gains get banked in a tape that is selling strength rather than extrapolating it. Gross equity 82%, no leverage, no perps — with the long end at 2007 highs, adding leverage to high-multiple growth is how you get carried out.]

SOX -19% MTD (worst month since 2008), $1trn of chip market cap gone, CXMT's IPO +466%, GPU rental prices -31% in three weeks, Alphabet's first negative-FCF quarter and Meta -10% after hours. Those four names are now roughly one position with four tickers, and their pairwise correlation breaks the 'lowest mutual correlation' half of my mandate far more badly than it satisfies the 'highest idiosyncratic vol' half. Owning them while shorting SPY/QQQ is worse than useless: they fall faster than the index they are hedged against, so the hedge only pays for part of the loss. I am cutting all four.

What replaces them is not a style drift, it is the same mandate re-screened for the current correlation regime. The redeployed capital goes into names whose volatility is genuinely company-specific and whose catalysts have just landed and been resolved with hard numbers: COF (new - Q2 beat, credit losses falling, Discover synergies on a 24-month clock, the highest-idiosyncratic-vol large-cap in a sector printing all-time highs), plus upsized HUM, PYPL, DLTR, CF, RCL. Nine names across eight sectors - fewer than twelve, but with a lower average pairwise correlation than the twelve I started with, which is the statistic the mandate actually cares about.

On sizing: I am not concentrating for its own sake. The edge here is cross-sectional, not single-name, so the honest expression is a broad basket, and I am spending the new freedom on the hedge mix instead. The old 60/40 SPY/QQQ split minimised residual vol when five longs loaded on the Nasdaq factor; with those longs gone, that logic is dead. I have moved to 21% QQQ / 16% SPY - a deliberate tilt toward QQQ because QQQ *is* the concentration index (top ten names dominate it) and the concentration unwind is the trade. RSP has beaten VOO by 3.7pp in a single month and is now ahead year to date; long a diversified equal-weight basket, short the cap-weighted concentration vehicle is the purest equity expression of long-dispersion/short-correlation available to me. Net index beta stays at roughly +0.02 (long-side beta ~42.8 against short-side ~40.8), so this is a spread bet, not a market bet.

I am keeping gross at 98% rather than reaching for leverage. The residual volatility of a properly hedged version of this book is ~7% annualised; the way to earn dollars from it is to own the right side of a 3.7pp/month cross-sectional spread, not to lever a hedged book into a tape where SOX is 19% down on the month and a violent oversold bounce into FOMC is a live risk. Standing orders reflect that asymmetry: take-profits on both index shorts so a snapback cannot hand back the concentration-unwind gain, and a stop plus take-profit on MRNA, which has a Q2 print on 31 July and an FDA flu decision on 5 August and is the one position sized deliberately small because the option skew says the long side is crowded. Filling on the next close rather than naming a date - I want out of the memory and AI-software complex now, not after another leg.]

First, I am exiting the XLU/D pair entirely. NextEra's all-stock acquisition of Dominion at a fixed 0.8138 exchange ratio, announced 2026-05-18 with state review beginning 2026-07-16, means D is now priced off a deal ratio and a merger spread rather than off the utility sector. The stationarity that earned that pair its 16% of gross - 27 mean-crossings, 46-day half-life - is an artefact of a lookback window that is mostly pre-announcement. It fails my own screen's drift and stationarity tests going forward, and it carried a 07-31 earnings event on the short leg. A pairs mandate is a bet on spreads that revert; this one has been converted into a merger-arb position I did not choose and do not want. Second, having freed that capital and with all concentration caps gone, I am pushing gross from 90% to the full 100% and redistributing across the five surviving pairs in proportion to conviction rather than in near-equal slices. WFC/BAC goes from 20% to 34.8% of gross - it is the widest spread (2.6sd, 14% to convergence), has the tightest hedge economics (betas 0.76 vs 0.77, so it is dollar-neutral and beta-neutral simultaneously), 17 mean-crossings and near-zero two-year drift, and its divergence event (07-14 earnings) is now behind it. I am deliberately not going further than that: WFC's NIM compression to 2.47% and two subpar quarters are a genuine fundamental reason the spread widened, and a 2.6sd gap with a story attached is exactly the kind that can widen to 3.5sd before it reverts. LOW/HD rises to 21.5% because it is the cleanest hedge I own (0.88 correlation, betas 0.65/0.68) with no event until mid-August. The QUAL+IWF vs MTUM triangle rises to 19.3% with IWF weighted above QUAL, since MTUM's +29% YTD on AI chips and its worst week of the year in early July are exactly the crowding decay I am positioned for. TSM/KLAC rises to 12.4% - larger, because KLAC's 07-28 print resolved the way I wanted (beat, but -5% on guidance) and both legs' earnings risk is now spent, but still the smallest sector pair because 2.15/2.70 betas make it the most dangerous spread I hold. MA/V is trimmed to 12.0%: it is the most stationary spread in the screen but only 4% spread vol, so it is the least productive use of scarce gross, and Visa's 2,600-job cost-cut announcement on 07-28 gives the short leg a margin story that can defend its premium. I am attaching no stop-losses or take-profits anywhere. On a beta-matched pairs book a stop on one leg converts a hedged spread into a naked directional position at precisely the moment the spread is widest - which for a mean-reversion strategy is when expected return is highest, not lowest. Standing orders would systematically monetise my worst entries and destroy the edge. Every pair remains individually beta-cancelled; removing XLU/D (whose 0.16 / -0.09 beta mismatch generated almost the entire prior +3.2% residual) leaves aggregate net SPY beta at roughly +0.07% of NAV, which is more faithful to the market-neutral mandate, not less. Turnover is about 48% of NAV at ~2bps a side, roughly a dime of cost against a book I expect to work over weeks. Cash goes to zero: 4% APY on idle cash is worth about 1bp a week, less than the reversion I expect from putting that capital into WFC/BAC.]

trades.fee_schedule: equities/ETFs 2bps (5bps leveraged, 12bps sub-$15) + 0.31bps SEC/TAF on sells; crypto spot 35bps; perps 7.5bps notional + 10% APR funding; short borrow 3% APR
trades.why:
Core of the book and my strongest measured window: XLI Jul-27 to Dec-31 averaged +5.39% at a 21/26-year (81%) hit rate, t=+2.49, 9/10 in the last decade, with the Nov-Dec leg alone at +4.68%, 81%, t=+3.78 and +1.59% versus SPY at t=+3.04. The new macro reinforces it — industrials are the cyclical least exposed to the AI-capex de-rating hitting tech, benefit from defense spend during an active Iran conflict, and are far less duration-sensitive than growth into a hiking scare. Raised from 18% because this is the one leg where my best statistic and the new regime agree without qualification. [Unrestricted-retail resize (2026-07-30, free internet + no sizing caps): The regime changed under the book three days after I set it, and it changed in a way that sorts my legs cleanly by measured conviction rather than forcing me off mandate. I am not abandoning calendar seasonality — I am re-sizing it so that weight concentrates where my Jul-27-to-year-end statistics and the new macro point the same direction, and drains from where they conflict.

CUT QQQ 20 -> 6. This was my largest position and my weakest evidence: QQQ minus SPY measured t=+1.35, the least significant statistic in my entire study, and I was carrying it at top weight purely because it was the 'growth core'. It now faces three simultaneous headwinds — the Nasdaq 100 is in correction, Meta missed by $1.04 with expenses +55% against revenue +28% and guided Q3 light, and rising long yields compress exactly this duration. I keep a 6% stub because QQQ's ABSOLUTE Jul-27 to Dec-31 window is still +3.97% at 20/26 years (77%) and Microsoft's Azure +43% shows the capex is at least buying revenue; it is the relative-to-SPY case, not the absolute case, that was thin. Sizing by measured conviction is the mandate, and this leg measured worst.

SIZE UP IEF SHORT 4 -> 17. This is now the single cleanest idea I own. My seasonal read was already the most extreme number in the study — intermediate Treasuries beat SPY in only 5/23 years (22%) over this window and in just 1 of the last 10, at -6.00% average. The macro has now arrived at the same conclusion from the other side: three FOMC dissents for a hike, ~60-79% odds of a hike by September, a $90 Brent inflation impulse, and long yields that ROSE on a hold. At 4% this leg could not earn anything even if it was perfectly right. At 17% it can. 3% borrow over five months costs ~0.2% of NAV, which is cheap for the only leg that pays off in the scenario that hurts everything else I own.

SIZE UP XLI 18 -> 20 and XLF 13 -> 16, KRE 6 -> 7. These carry my best measured windows (XLI +5.39%, 21/26 years, t=+2.49, with Nov-Dec at t=+3.78 and t=+3.04 versus SPY; XLF +5.04% at 20/26 and 9/10 in the last decade at +8.94%; KRE the highest-return sleeve at +7.24%, t=+2.28, 8/10 last decade at +10.14%). Crucially the macro now reinforces rather than merely permits them: a bear steepener with the Fed on hold and long yields rising is the textbook environment for bank net interest margin, and industrials are the cyclical least exposed to the AI-capex de-rating while benefiting from defense spending in an active Middle East conflict. Financials and industrials were both named in the broad-participation breadth data.

SIZE UP GLD 13 -> 15. My cleanest non-equity seasonal (+3.54% Jul-27 to Oct-27, t=+1.69, +3.13% versus SPY at t=+1.80) now has a live geopolitical and inflation catalyst stacked on top, and the tell that matters is that gold rose 0.94% on the hawkish day while yields rose. Positioning is also far cleaner at $4,066 than at the January $5,595 peak. This is simultaneously my seasonal leg and the hedge that pays if the September hike breaks my cyclical longs.

HOLD XLU 9 -> 8. I expected to cut this as a bond proxy into a hiking scare, but the breadth data argued me out of it: 90% of XLU constituents sit above their 200-day EMA, the strongest of all 11 sectors, because the bid is AI power demand rather than duration. Combined with a positive measured Sep-30 to Oct-31 window (19/26 years, 8/10 in the last decade) I keep it near full size, trimming a point for rate risk.

DROP XLP 5 -> 0. Painful because it had my highest t-statistic (t=+3.32 absolute, t=+3.93 for Nov-Dec), but that edge is concentrated in the Oct-31 to Dec-31 leg, and staples face input-cost compression from a $90 oil shock in the meantime. This is a timing decision, not a rejection: I intend to re-enter it with cash at the November rotation, which is exactly what the dry powder is for.

TRIM EFA SHORT 5 -> 5 (unchanged). I nearly cut this. The seasonal case is genuinely good (positive in only 9/24 years, 2/10 in the last decade at -2.65%), but half of its mechanism was dollar strength and DXY is stuck near 101 rather than breaking out — and a US-led tech correction can actually flatter less tech-heavy foreign indices. Holding at existing size rather than adding, since its natural pair (long QQQ) just shrank by two thirds.

CASH 7 -> 6. I release one point to fund the IEF short while preserving essentially all pre-committed dry powder for the Oct-1 and Nov-1 rotations, when XLP and the mid/small-cap shift come back on.

Standing orders: I tighten KRE's stop from -25% to -20%, because the original -25% was calibrated to the 2008 drawdown as a pure beta event, whereas the live risk is credit stress from a hike landing on top of an oil shock, which would show up faster. I add a -18% stop on the QQQ stub and a -12% stop on EFA. I attach a -10% stop to the IEF short: if intermediate Treasuries rally 10% against me that is a flight-to-quality recession event, in which case my industrials, financials and regional banks are all bleeding too and I want that leg closed rather than doubling the correlation. I put a +30% take-profit on GLD to bank an extreme war spike, set deliberately wide so it does not decapitate the hedge during ordinary strength. Taking the next available fill rather than naming a date — I am adding to cyclicals into a flush, which is the right side of this print, and waiting for a bounce to sell my QQQ cut would be over-cleverness.]

2x Energy Select — the core. 32 points buys 64% effective XLE exposure. The trade is the dislocation: on 29 July crude gapped +6.2% (WTI $84.18, Brent $89.43) on the collapse of the US-Iran ceasefire and fresh strikes, and XLE rose only +1.88%. Energy equities are still discounting crude far below spot after five months of a shut Strait of Hormuz, which gives me both the convergence upside and the downside cushion (2026 downside capture on crude down-days was 0.27x — equities cannot hand back a move they never made). XLE is the #1 sector of 2026 at +37.3% YTD and +9.02% in July while XLK fell 6.81%, the widest monthly split since January 2022. ERX printed +3.78% against XLE's +1.88% — exactly 2.0x, no measurable decay. The -30% stop caps this leg at 9.6% of NAV and corresponds to roughly a -15% XLE break. [Unrestricted-retail resize (2026-07-30, free internet + no sizing caps): The thesis got materially stronger and my own book is what is holding it back. Since 27 July the account has made +0.36% while the mandate's core driver went vertical — crude +6.2% in a single session on the collapse of the ceasefire, with Hormuz still shut. The energy legs did their job (ERX +3.78% on the day) and the diversifiers ate the gains: AAPL -0.56%, XLV -0.61%, RTX -1.52%. So I am cutting the three legs that are no longer earning their weight and putting the capital into the two I actually believe in.

CUT AAPL (7% to 0). It was bought as a hedge against the tech unwind reversing. It has stopped being that hedge: XLK fell 6.81% in July while AAPL made an all-time high and crossed $5trn. It has decoupled, so it will not protect me if semis keep unwinding, and it is not correlated to anything I need if energy works. On top of that it is a binary print tonight, at an all-time high, into a consensus price target 5% BELOW spot. That is a coin flip I am not paid to take.

CUT RTX (7% to 0). This is the cleanest sell signal in the packet. RTX beat by 14% and RAISED full-year guidance on 23 July, and then fell — including -1.52% on the day crude gapped 6% on fresh Middle East strikes. A defence name that will not rally on a beat-and-raise INTO a widening war is fully priced. The 'coherent with the supply-shock regime' argument is true and irrelevant if the market refuses to pay for it.

CUT XLF (11% to 0). It was the one leg with no thesis of its own — its stated job was to supply positive SPY beta so the book was not a pure short-market expression. I am scored on flat dollars, not tracking error, so paying 11 points for beta cosmetics is a waste. It is also the least coherent leg with the mandate: an oil shock at $89 Brent is stagflationary, and the NIM benefit from rising long yields is offset by the credit cost of a squeezed consumer.

ADD ERX 22% to 32% (64% effective XLE). The single best piece of information I found is that XLE rose 1.88% on a 6.2% crude day. The equity market is pricing this as temporary and crude as mean-reverting; Hormuz has been shut since March and the ceasefire has already failed once. That skepticism is simultaneously my upside (equities have to converge) and my downside cushion (they cannot give back a move they never made — 2026 downside capture on crude down-days was 0.27x). ERX again realised exactly 2.0x with no decay, so I am getting the leverage cleanly. Stop stays at -30%, which caps this leg at 9.6% of NAV and corresponds to roughly a -15% XLE break.

ADD MPC 9% to 16%. Highest-conviction single name and the only near-dated catalyst I own: 4 August, consensus EPS +184-199% y/y on record cracks, with management having pulled 40% of annual turnarounds into Q1 specifically to run at 94% utilisation into this window. The sell-side average PT of $301.59 is stale and sits below spot while the two most recent revisions are Goldman $376 and TD Cowen $357. Crack spreads are a genuinely different driver from crude beta (-0.16 correlation to SPY), so this is not just more ERX. I am sizing it BEFORE the print because the print is the reason. The -25% stop caps the leg at 4.0% of NAV, which is the price of admission for a stock up 71% YTD.

ADD XLY SHORT 13% to 17%. The purest expression of the whole thesis and now doing double duty: $89 Brent is a consumer tax, and 39% of this ETF is AMZN plus TSLA — the two names carrying both the consumer squeeze and the AI-valuation de-rating that took XLK down 6.81% in July. At -0.38 correlation to XLE it is additive to the energy core rather than an offset, and it is my only real protection if the market breaks broadly. [Weekly desk 2026-08-01: I got the biggest thing wrong and the cost of admitting it one session in is about 0.2bp, so I am admitting it. My 18% SMH short was explicitly justified by a live catalyst - hyperscaler capex doubt plus SK Hynix's guidance miss - and that catalyst did not fade, it inverted: Microsoft's AI business grew 123% with Azure accelerating, Amazon's cloud beat, Big Tech capex is tracking ~$650bn for 2026, and SK Hynix and Samsung printed their best days on record. That is a demand confirmation for the exact cohort I am short, not sentiment noise, and the split reaction - Meta -8% for refusing a capex outlook on the same day MSFT had its best session since 2008 - shows a market discriminating between AI spenders and AI beneficiaries rather than de-rating duration wholesale, with semis on the receiving end of the spend. What survives is only the weak half of my case, 'it went up 80% so it must fall', which is not an edge and has bankrupted better shorts than me. So the hedge goes back to the mandate's own word - SMALL - at 6%, exactly where it stood before I tripled it. I am not flipping to long semis and I am not switching vehicles: I checked ARKK and it is flat over twelve months, so it is not stretched and would be a worse short. Still cheap at 11x with 13% ROTCE, so I hold it, but I will not size up on a premise I have just disproved. The remaining 9 points go to cash at 4%, deliberately: cutting a 12-point short is itself a large increase in net long exposure, from about 54% to about 69%, and I do not want to take that step up in directionality into a Fed with two-thirds odds of a September hike, a 5.28% 30-year, and a live Strait of Hormuz conflict. PFE, VZ, VLO and MO are untouched - nothing about their theses changed in two sessions, and PFE's 8/4 print is a reason to sit still rather than trade.]

The carry shrank and the tail fattened simultaneously, so the leg goes. It is a negative-carry structure whose best environment is chop and whose worst is trend, and an oil-and-rates shock is a trending catalyst, so the case only got weaker. Closing both costs about 26% turnover at ~2-2.5bps, roughly $0.07, and it is economically positive from day one: I stop paying 0.42%/yr of NAV in borrow and start earning 4% on the cash. Net result is a simpler book, lower gross, no borrow, more cash yield, and my two best-evidenced legs plus a cheap hedge.]

Second, the shock I repositioned around on 30 July did not persist — SPY has fully round-tripped it and IWM is printing new highs — so the reason I gave for cutting small-cap beta has been falsified by price, which is the only evidence my mandate lets me weigh. [Weekly desk 2026-08-08: The insurance I bought on 30 July expired unused and is now costing me. I sized this book for a capex scare broadening into an opex scare, and instead all three prints I was carrying resolved bullish — NET beat, raised and closed at an all-time high, DDOG beat and raised FY guide to $4.45-4.47bn, and IWM finished within 0.5% of its 52-week high — so small-cap and software leadership is intact rather than broken. Two lines were built for the scenario that did not arrive and must shrink. CRWD was explicitly held as the defensive line if software budgets got cut; that call was wrong, and it now trades ~11% ABOVE its 53-analyst consensus target of $193 after an 80% six-month run, which is the worst forward risk/reward in the book regardless of how good the business is. NU is cut not on thesis but on calendar: it is the single name with a print inside the coming week (13 August) and I do not want 16% of NAV riding one Brazilian quarter when I cannot control the gap. HOOD comes down two points and stays the joint-largest: it is the only name my rate view helps rather than hurts and prediction-market revenue just went up tenfold, but it is -11.7% over 52 weeks and I will not keep adding to a persistent laggard on a story. Cash goes 18% to 13% because 4% on idle money is a poor trade against a confirmed uptrend, while still leaving a real buffer given I could not verify this week's rates and Fed news and the book has already seen a -10.29% drawdown.]

I am taking this in bullion rather than GDX/GDXJ deliberately. The miners have been squeezing shorts hard, which tells me the direction is right but the entry is extended, and stacking mining operating leverage on top of a 2x levered energy fund would concentrate variance in precisely the thing I am trying to reduce. At ~15% annualised vol a 20% weight carries materially less portfolio variance than the 26% ERX position it partly replaces. The -18% stop is set wide on purpose: it caps the leg at 3.6% of NAV and is far enough out that a headline-driven spike will not shake me out of a hedge, but it is close enough that a genuine break of the record-high structure — which would mean the rate-cut thesis died — takes me out. trades.why: The new core, and the point of the whole rebalance. Cboe implied correlation is at its lowest in at least 23 years - COR3M ~9-10 against a 52-week range of 9.29-11.95, COR1M printing 8.7-9.93, expected average single-stock correlation ~23%. Index variance is approximately average constituent variance times correlation, so at these readings the S&P realizes 13.49% (20d, close-to-close) while its average member realizes far more. That is diversification benefit at a two-decade maximum, and it is free. Every other way I have owned equity in this book paid for its low volatility: USMV pays in surrendered expected return (+5.21% YTD vs SPLV's +9.98% and an index at record highs), SPLV pays by concentrating 25.4% in utilities. SPY pays nothing for it. In a genuinely high-dispersion regime the correct long-only expression is to own the index rather than its components, because dispersion is exactly what makes the wrapper safer than its contents - and I had been drawing the opposite conclusion from the same data, buying low-vol stocks when the dispersion I identified was an argument for the index. Sized at 40% rather than higher for two reasons: the melt-up ran on a jobs contraction, which is the rate channel doing the work rather than earnings, and the 15-16 Sep FOMC still carries a 44%-priced hike under Warsh. The -18% stop is deliberately wide - it is a regime-break brake, not a trading stop, because VIXY is the actual hedge and stacking a tight stop on top of a convex hedge is double-paying for the same protection and inviting a whipsaw out of the position at the worst moment. [Weekly desk 2026-08-08: Two things moved enough to force this, and they point the same way. First, the volatility risk premium has closed: VIX 15.15 against SPY 20d realized 13.49% is ~1.7 points, versus a ~3-4 point norm, so index vol is no longer expensive - and Cboe implied correlation sits at a 23-year low (COR3M ~9-10, 52-week range 9.29-11.95), which is a bounded, mean-reverting quantity that can only normalise upward. Cheaper insurance against a denser calendar - CPI 12-Aug, a stalled Hormuz fee dispute with Brent at $80, and a 15-16 Sep FOMC where a Warsh hike is still 44% priced after payrolls printed -23k with 103k of downward revisions. Second, and this is the correction I owe myself: I have been conflating vol targeting with owning low-vol stocks. Vol targeting scales exposure to the INDEX by the index's realized vol. USMV and SPLV buy their low vol by surrendering expected return and by parking 25% of SPLV in utilities ahead of a live hike; the index buys its low vol from diversification, which is free and is at a 23-year maximum precisely because correlation is at a 23-year low. At COR3M ~10 the S&P realizes 13.5% while its average constituent realizes far more - that makes SPY the cheapest carrier of equity risk in my universe right now, not USMV. My book was carrying only ~40 SPY-equivalent betas into a low-correlation, low-index-vol tape and made +0.97% while the index made +3.58% and tech made +7.2%. Three trends I owned rolled over and two I did not own turned up. A trend that cannot rally on its own best news is over, and a shrinking payroll count explains why. So XLE goes to zero and PDBC is cut from 24% to a residual. Second, I close the SMH short outright. Last week I wrote that I was applying the trend filter honestly; applying it honestly today means admitting that a name up 103% over twelve months, 27.8% above its 200-day, that just rose 7.8% in a week, is not a downtrend a trend book gets to be short. The intermediate dip was the countertrend, not the trend, and I was on the wrong side of my own rule. Third, the redeployment. EFA is the cleanest uptrend on my entire screen — positive on every horizon from one week to twelve months, above both moving averages — and a Fed cutting into a weak dollar is the structural tailwind for ex-US equity, so it becomes a core leg. IWM gets the equity-momentum slot: 13.3% above its 200-day and beating the S&P year-to-date, and small caps are the most direct expression of the rate-cut repricing. XLF adds trend plus dividend carry with far better credit quality than KRE, which I screened and rejected because regional-bank credit into a contracting labour market is the wrong risk to be paid for. JEPI is upgraded from a grudging stub to a real weight because it now clears the filter it failed on 7/31 — it has reclaimed its 200-day (+4.1%) and option-writing income is exactly the right carry to own if this melt-up turns choppy. DBMF stays the structural core even though it went nowhere this week; the whole point of a managed-futures sleeve is that it re-positions across the regime turn without my having to call each leg. BTC is cut to zero and only ETH keeps a crypto stub: both are still below their 200-days and down 44% and 55% on the year, and if I only get to hold one broken trend it should be the one 6.7% above its 50-day rather than 2.6%.]

trades.fee_schedule: equities/ETFs 2bps (5bps leveraged, 12bps sub-$15) + 0.31bps SEC/TAF on sells; crypto spot 35bps; perps 7.5bps notional + 10% APR funding; short borrow 3% APR
trades.why: PEAD whose catalyst hardened into contract, unchanged and untouched. The signal is intact and still inside its window, which closes ~08-20: +10.54% gap 2026-07-23 on 3.3x volume, prior 20d +12.9%, ADV $511m, every filter of the n=658 rule met (mean +2.81% raw, t=+4.74; +2.06% market-hedged, t=+3.69). The reason this carries the largest weight is unchanged: the 07-30/08-03 Army award of $58.6bn for PAC-3 MSE — the largest Patriot contract ever — converts April's $4.7bn one-year deal into an FY2026-2032 multiyear running to March 2035 that triples interceptor output by 2030, and it is exactly the segment whose +20% revenue print caused the gap I bought. This week added only confirmation of the same production story (successful Next Generation Interceptor Stage 2 static fire on 08-10, a new missile-technology product centre), which is not a new catalyst and does not justify adding. Stop 10%, no take-profit, because my own test showed a take-profit cuts the mean from +2.81% to +1.37%. [Weekly desk 2026-08-15: Two things expired and one thing was proved out; nothing else changed, so I moved exactly those. The ISRG and NFLX capitulation legs reached the end of the 20-session horizon their edge is measured over on 08-14, and both delivered inside it (ISRG 378.81 to 394.51, NFLX 74.14 to 78.16 in the final week alone). Holding them past 08-14 would convert a tested edge into an untested directional bet on two high-multiple names at a record index, which is precisely the thing my process exists to avoid, so both come out at expiry rather than on a view. That frees 12%. I redeploy it in two places. First, TEAM from 9% to 13%: I explicitly sized that leg small because a 35% single-day gap was the most extreme in this book's history and I expected severe post-gap volatility, and one full week of tape has partially retired that concern — 149.07 to 162.22 with the range never breaking below 151 and no reversal day — while it is now the only position whose window (to ~09-04) survives past 08-21. That is a haircut being removed for an observed reason, not a conviction upsize. Second, a 6% NVDA pre-announcement leg into the 08-26 print, the one mandate leg the book has been missing, sized small precisely because the announcement premium is a published effect rather than one of my own measured statistics. I add nothing from this week's gap tape despite a clean-looking SMCI setup, because it can only be filled at a three-session lag and I disqualified SHOP and PLTR on that identical test seven days ago. Cash rises to 14%, which is deliberate: almost the entire book rolls off its measured window by 08-21 and dry powder into that rebuild is worth more than a forced trade at 4% on the balance.]

With Hormuz traffic near 5% of pre-conflict levels and OPEC spare capacity down to roughly 2.5M bpd, the sector and the commodity are now priced consistently and my measurable edge is gone. I keep a 6% stub rather than covering entirely because energy at +38% YTD is still unambiguously the crowded top-decile winner cluster this mandate is built to lean against, and because a Hormuz reopening deal was close enough to be reported once and would deflate the entire risk premium in days. But 13% of a short against a live physical supply disruption with non-linear upside is not a mean-reversion position, it is a bet on a war ending, and the -15% stop stays tight precisely because I no longer have a reason to give this leg room.

[Weekly desk 2026-08-15: Two of my five spreads stopped qualifying this week for opposite reasons, and the reason I trimmed a third was erased by new information. MA/V hit its exit condition: MA rose 15% on a clean Q2 (net revenue +14%, adj EPS $5.04 vs $4.77, guidance raised) and the target-implied gap that got me in collapsed from 9 points to 2.6. A mandate built on stationary spreads takes the convergence when it arrives; holding on hoping a mean-reverting spread overshoots is not the trade I described, and MA's move was earnings, not noise, so I will not flip the sign either. The November reconstitution will also drag MTUM's beta toward Micron's ~2.2 against the ~1.5 my triangle is matched to, and I cannot re-hedge drift from inside a fund; better to own no beta mismatch than a small one I cannot fix. Against that I add to the two spreads whose evidence improved. WFC/BAC widened against me on price while widening in my favour on substance: BAC printed a fresh 52-week high at $65.20 and its consensus upside fell to 7.1% while WFC's held at 14.3%, so the convergence gap went from 5.7 to 7.2 points on the book's best stationarity evidence (17 mean-crossings, ~zero two-year drift, 0.80 correlation). LOW/HD is the honest reversal: last week I cut it from 21.5% of gross precisely because consensus upside had converged to ~14% vs ~15% and I refused to pay for a two-day earnings window with no edge in it. That gap is now 9.1 points (LOW +19.5% with the stock near its 52-week low, HD +10.4% on freshly RAISED targets), LOW's bar into the print is lower (EPS guided down yoy on deal costs), and HD's CEO is on medical leave. The condition that justified the trim is gone, so I restore the size rather than pretend consistency means never changing back. TSM/KLAC stays exactly where it is because the week cut both ways — Lam lifting CY2026 WFE to the low $150bns says the cycle peak is higher than my short assumed, while AMAT dropping 6% on record revenue and a 51% growth guide says the multiple, not the fundamentals, is the binding constraint. Mixed evidence is a reason to hold a position, not to resize it. Gross falls from 90.5% to 77.7% and cash rises to 22.3%: I cut two sub-books and found no replacement that passed my screen — XLU/D is now a merger-arb instrument because of the NextEra deal, CVX/XOM trade at identical forward multiples, GS/MS is a one-point gap — so the unused gross earns 4% instead of buying a spread I have not measured. I attach no stops or take-profits anywhere: on a beta-matched pair a per-leg percentage stop is triggered by the market's direction rather than the spread's, and firing one leg converts a hedged relative-value position into an outright directional bet, which is a worse outcome than the loss it was meant to cap. Everything fills at the next open — I want the MA/V convergence banked before it can give back, and the LOW/HD size on before the 08-18 print.]

This leg no longer needs the macro to do the work, but for the first time in a month the macro is doing it anyway. [Weekly desk 2026-08-15: Last week I wrote that my error was re-sizing this book on a macro overlay that then inverted inside five sessions. I am making exactly one substantive trade, and it is driven by a fact about a specific sleeve rather than by a macro regime call. trades.why:

Last week I argued that at a 23-year implied-correlation low the S&P wrapper is safer than its contents, because index variance is average constituent variance scaled by correlation - and then bought SPY, which is not what that identity describes. The identity is an equal-weight statement. RSP realizes 9.79% at 20d and 10.92% at 60d against SPY's 13.33% and 13.93%: the equal-weighted index collects roughly a quarter less volatility from exactly the dispersion I identified, because SPY's ~40% megacap concentration in names realizing 25-45% (QQQ 23.64, XLK 32.73, SMH 46.39) claws most of the correlation benefit back. I refused to act on 20 days of realized vol alone, so I checked the full year: RSP returned +21.8% against SPY's +22.0% - the return is not being surrendered, which is the whole point and the thing USMV and SPLV cannot say - with a shallower max drawdown (-7.9% vs -8.9%) and roughly 68% average downside capture on SPY's eight worst sessions. Same return, less volatility, less drawdown, better crash behaviour, at 20d, 60d and 1y. This is what a high-dispersion regime is supposed to pay a long-only book, and I was leaving it on the table. The -14% stop is a regime brake rather than a trading stop, set to the same ~1.4 annual sigma as SPY's -18% given RSP's lower realized vol, so the two core legs are stopped at equivalent severity rather than at equivalent-looking numbers. [Weekly desk 2026-08-15: Two pieces of my own evidence turned against last week's construction and one turned against last week's arithmetic, so this is a correction rather than a view change - the regime call (calm index, violent components) is unchanged and this book expresses it better.

First, the arithmetic. I built a 40% SPY core on 'index variance equals average constituent variance times correlation', arguing the cap-weighted wrapper is safer than its contents at a 23-year correlation low. That identity is an equal-weight identity. RSP realizes 9.79% at 20d and 10.92% at 60d against SPY's 13.33% and 13.93%, on the same tape in the same window - the equal-weighted index captures the diversification benefit I was describing while SPY's megacap concentration consumes most of it. I checked this was not a 20-day artefact before acting on it: over the trailing year RSP returned +21.8% against SPY's +22.0% with a smaller max drawdown (-7.9% vs -8.9%) and roughly 68% average downside capture across SPY's eight worst days. Identical return, a quarter less volatility, at all three horizons. If my mandate is return per unit of realized vol, RSP is simply the better vehicle for the exact thesis I already hold, so 30% moves to RSP and SPY keeps 20% because I am correcting an expression, not abandoning cap-weighted beta entirely.

Second, the carry. VIXM/VIXY moved +3.9% in five sessions against a ~1.1%/week three-month average; netting each ETF's beta to spot leaves roughly a point a week of excess front-month decay, about 50% annualised. On 08-08 I explicitly justified upsizing VIXY to 11% on the claim that compressed contango had cut my roll cost to a third-to-a-half of the 43.8%/yr underwritten at entry. That claim is now false by my own measurement. Separately, the value case has thinned: VIX 14.25 against 10d realized 11.64% is 2.6 points of premium, near normal, and realized is falling faster than implied. I am not abandoning the hedge - VVIX at 87 is cheap convexity, SKEW rose to 138 in a week VIX fell, and the 15-16 Sep FOMC is a dated live binary inside my horizon - but a leg whose price of carry has doubled while its value case thinned should shrink to true insurance size, so 11% goes to 7% with the take-profit untouched.

Third, SPLV. I kept it for tech-free diversification, but its protection is a rates bet and rates went the wrong way: ^TNX to 4.70 with ^IRX pinned at 3.70, a long-end-led steepening, which is precisely the inflation-expectations move an +7.9% Brent week produces. XLU -2.55% and SPLV -0.57% on the month confirm it. Once RSP is in the book, SPLV's broad-diversification role is redundant and only its concentrated utilities bet remains, so I exit it.

What replaces it is the reason I am comfortable cutting the vol sleeve. XLE printed positive on five of SPY's eight worst days of the trailing year - better crash behaviour than SPLV's four of eight - while returning +49.2% over that year against SPLV's +6.2%. It is long the one macro shock actually running (Brent +7.9%, XLE +7.7%, USO +7.3% in a week the S&P gained 0.4% and VIX fell), and an energy-led inflation impulse is the single state where SPY, USMV and cash all lose together and only my hedges help. Sized at just 7% because it realizes 24.5% vol and because a leg that ran 7.7% in five sessions deserves respect, not enthusiasm. The net effect is a book with the same equity beta, materially less realized volatility, a hedge that earns rather than bleeds, and 18% cash at 4% into a live September Fed.]

Keeping 20% means the concentration question costs me a fraction of the book rather than all of it if I am wrong about which wrapper wins from here. I checked this was not a 20-day artefact before acting on it: over the trailing year RSP returned +21.8% against SPY's +22.0% with a smaller max drawdown (-7.9% vs -8.9%) and roughly 68% average downside capture across SPY's eight worst days. Identical return, a quarter less volatility, at all three horizons. If my mandate is return per unit of realized vol, RSP is simply the better vehicle for the exact thesis I already hold, so 30% moves to RSP and SPY keeps 20% because I am correcting an expression, not abandoning cap-weighted beta entirely.

Second, the carry. VIXM/VIXY moved +3.9% in five sessions against a ~1.1%/week three-month average; netting each ETF's beta to spot leaves roughly a point a week of excess front-month decay, about 50% annualised. On 08-08 I explicitly justified upsizing VIXY to 11% on the claim that compressed contango had cut my roll cost to a third-to-a-half of the 43.8%/yr underwritten at entry. That claim is now false by my own measurement. Separately, the value case has thinned: VIX 14.25 against 10d realized 11.64% is 2.6 points of premium, near normal, and realized is falling faster than implied. I am not abandoning the hedge - VVIX at 87 is cheap convexity, SKEW rose to 138 in a week VIX fell, and the 15-16 Sep FOMC is a dated live binary inside my horizon - but a leg whose price of carry has doubled while its value case thinned should shrink to true insurance size, so 11% goes to 7% with the take-profit untouched.

Third, SPLV. I kept it for tech-free diversification, but its protection is a rates bet and rates went the wrong way: ^TNX to 4.70 with ^IRX pinned at 3.70, a long-end-led steepening, which is precisely the inflation-expectations move an +7.9% Brent week produces. XLU -2.55% and SPLV -0.57% on the month confirm it. Once RSP is in the book, SPLV's broad-diversification role is redundant and only its concentrated utilities bet remains, so I exit it.

What replaces it is the reason I am comfortable cutting the vol sleeve. XLE printed positive on five of SPY's eight worst days of the trailing year - better crash behaviour than SPLV's four of eight - while returning +49.2% over that year against SPLV's +6.2%. It is long the one macro shock actually running (Brent +7.9%, XLE +7.7%, USO +7.3% in a week the S&P gained 0.4% and VIX fell), and an energy-led inflation impulse is the single state where SPY, USMV and cash all lose together and only my hedges help. Sized at just 7% because it realizes 24.5% vol and because a leg that ran 7.7% in five sessions deserves respect, not enthusiasm. The net effect is a book with the same equity beta, materially less realized volatility, a hedge that earns rather than bleeds, and 18% cash at 4% into a live September Fed.]

trades.fee_schedule: equities/ETFs 2bps (5bps leveraged, 12bps sub-$15) + 0.31bps SEC/TAF on sells; crypto spot 35bps; perps 7.5bps notional + 10% APR funding; short borrow 3% APR
trades.why: Raised 16% -> 22% and now the top weight, because the one number I sized this on has moved decisively in my favour for a second straight week. I wrote that 16% was justified by Brent at $88-90. Brent is $94.39, with WTI $87.06 and Murban $103.50, on mounting Iran risk and continuing Hormuz shipping disruption, against an IEA forecast of the widest global supply deficit in five years, Venezuelan export delays, and a US posture that has not softened. The distinction from the round-trip that cost me money is that I cut on a single de-escalation headline; I am adding on two consecutive weeks of confirming price action plus a supply-balance forecast, which is evidence rather than a news item. The company leg was never the question: record quarterly net income of $20.59bn up 50% year over year, production up on Hess and the Permian, record US refinery throughput, and a 20-year Microsoft data-centre power agreement that monetises the AI buildout without paying an AI multiple for it. At $205.27 it is 13.26x forward with a 3.47% yield, beta 0.49, and a $217.88 consensus from 25 analysts at Buy implying 6.1% more. This is the cheapest, lowest-beta, dividend-paying way to own the crude dislocation and it is the book's inflation hedge. I tighten the stop from -18% to -15% deliberately: a 22% weight sitting on a driver a single Hormuz de-escalation could reverse does not deserve the same wide stop it had at 16%, and the whole lesson of last month is that the exit should be pre-committed rather than improvised under a headline. [Weekly desk 2026-08-22: The single macro variable driving this book escalated for a second consecutive week and I am underweight it, while two legs decayed on their own stated terms - so I rotate weight toward the confirmed driver instead of leaving the book configured for last week's world. Brent went $88.52 -> $94.39 on mounting Iran risk and Hormuz disruption; I sized CVX at 16% explicitly on Brent being $88-90, so 16% is now stale by my own arithmetic and it goes to 22%. That add is funded by exiting MO entirely and trimming VZ, not by spending cash: gross stays 80%, cash 20%, so this is a rotation, not a risk increase. I exit MO because last week I wrote in plain words that it survives 'purely as ballast and carry' and is 'not a discount trade and I will not pretend it is one' - a Hold-rated name with 5.9% to target, flat revenue, narrowed guidance and an inverted duration argument (TLT at 22-year lows) does not belong in a concentrated deep-value book, and holding it now would be sentiment rather than analysis. I trim VZ 13% -> 11% because the discount is nearly closed at 4.3% to target while the exact risk I named as the reason to keep it small - SpaceX direct-to-cell - became a live tape-moving story with Starlink Mobile's wireless push; when my named bear case converts from hypothetical to live, weight comes down, and applying that rule only to losers would be self-serving. I raise the SMH short 5% -> 7% because last week I refused to add for one specific stated reason: the market had been handed my de-rating mechanism and rejected it. This week it accepted it - SMH fell 4.7% with the long end still at its lows - so the condition I set for adding was met, and a larger hedge is warranted anyway now that oil beta is bigger. I HOLD PFE at 20% rather than applying my past-target harvest rule, because that rule triggers on trading ABOVE consensus (VLO, 10.4% above) and PFE is 1.9% BELOW it, on targets that visibly have not caught up to the raised guidance; at 10.1x forward against a ~19x sector it remains an absolute-multiple holding, not a closed target gap, and it is the only leg with no crude beta and no AI duration, which is what keeps this from becoming a one-factor energy book. I HOLD C at 14% despite it being the only loser: the credit risk I named got genuinely worse ($94 Brent onto negative payrolls, and the tape marked it down 5.5%), but the curve-steepener tailwind I named got genuinely stronger and the discount widened to 11.3x with 17.4% to target on the cheapest large-cap US bank - those offset honestly, so I neither add nor dress up a cosmetic 1% trim as a decision. I HOLD VLO at 6% and refuse to chase it 1% off its 52-week high and 10.4% above consensus even though cracks are blowing out further, because that is exactly the mean-reverting cash flow I said it was; the honest way to buy more of this shock is CVX. I tighten CVX's stop from -18% to -15% because a 22% weight riding a geopolitical driver that one de-escalation headline can reverse is precisely the exposure that cost me the CVX round-trip, and it deserves a pre-committed exit rather than an improvised one. Turnover is roughly 15% of notional at ~2bps a side, about 0.3bp of NAV - immaterial against the repositioning.]

trades.fee_schedule: equities/ETFs 2bps (5bps leveraged, 12bps sub-$15) + 0.31bps SEC/TAF on sells; crypto spot 35bps; perps 7.5bps notional + 10% APR funding; short borrow 3% APR
trades.why: The book's anchor, raised from 26 with money taken from one and two rungs below it. This week gave me the cleanest argument I have had for seniority: the loan market's tail is repricing hard — CCC spreads out 300bp+ year to date to ~1,024bp — while BB spreads actually tightened and the index average still reads a benign ~271bp. When an average is that far from its own tail, the honest trade is to own the part of the structure the tail cannot reach. AAA CLO tranches sit above 600+ deals' worth of subordination with thirty years and no AAA default, at SOFR+~120bp with effectively zero duration. It is also the only leg indifferent to both binaries in front of me: if Warsh is hawkish on 28 August the coupon simply resets higher, and if the 30-year keeps making 19-year highs it owns no duration to lose. Flows agree — AUM is $30.0bn, up from $27bn a fortnight ago, and the fund returned 4.89% over the year against a 4.91% yield, meaning it is paying its coupon out of income rather than principal, which is exactly what SPHY and CLOZ are not doing. I take the criticism that the spread over 4% cash is only about a point; that point is why this is 30 and not 40, with the rest sitting in actual cash. Wide -10% stop because the only genuine risk here is a liquidity gap and a tight stop would whipsaw me out of the safest income I own. [Weekly desk 2026-08-22: Two facts changed enough to move real weight, and one of my hedges is gone. First, the high-yield average is concealing a broken distribution: the index OAS is ~271bp near the tights while CCC & lower is at ~1,024bp and CCC loan spreads have widened 300bp+ this year against BB loans that actually TIGHTENED. That is late-cycle bifurcation, and both my sub-senior credit legs are already paying for it out of principal — SPHY returned 5.65% over a year on a 7.20% coupon, CLOZ 5.05% on a 7.22% coupon. The right response is not to leave credit but to move up the capital structure inside it, so SPHY goes to zero, CLOZ is cut, and the proceeds go to AAA CLO paper that sits above the tranche where the tail is repricing. Second, the specific event I paid carry to avoid got smaller while the force I was ignoring got bigger: hike odds fell 42%->33% on a benign 3.4%/2.5% CPI, but the 30-year printed a 19-YEAR high and the Treasury responded by doubling long-end buybacks — soft financial repression that is dollar-negative, and DXY is at a three-month low of 98.80. I underpaid for EM local carry last week on the opposite call, so I restore it. Third, I am not replacing the BTC short. It cost me ~2.5% of NAV stopping at $78,182, and re-shorting an asset six days after its biggest weekly gain since March 2024, into $56bn of open interest with fresh leverage rebuilding, would be a grudge rather than a thesis. The risk I actually need to blunt before Warsh speaks on 28 August is a simultaneous mark-down of every spread leg I own, and 19% cash at 4% APY does that at zero carrying cost instead of 3x leverage that can gap through its stop.]

My objection has been that writing index calls is worth size at VIX 18 and not at VIX 14, and VIX is 15.13 — better than the 14.25 low but still cheap, so I am not adding. What changed is the underlying: after three straight weeks of record highs the S&P fell 1.4% with technology down more than 3%, and a capped-upside, premium-collecting structure is at its best in exactly that flat-to-down tape rather than in the melt-up that was punishing it. Two honest caveats keep it small. The 11.85% distribution carries a 331% payout ratio, so a large part of what I am collecting is return of capital rather than harvested premium; and the fund is 8.25% NVIDIA, 6.74% Apple and 5.56% Microsoft, which is concentrated single-name beta wearing an income label. It stays at 4 because the mandate calls for an equity-premium sleeve and monthly distributions still clear cash. For the same reason I again decline to add SVXY: with VIX near the year's low, selling variance insurance is selling it at the cheapest possible price.

trades.fee_schedule: equities/ETFs 2bps (5bps leveraged, 12bps sub-$15) + 0.31bps SEC/TAF on sells; crypto spot 35bps; perps 7.5bps notional + 10% APR funding; short borrow 3% APR
trades.why: Biotech, and the leg that just proved the mandate. Intismeran autogene (mRNA-4157) with Merck met both its primary recurrence-free survival endpoint and the secondary distant metastasis-free survival endpoint in Phase 3 adjuvant melanoma on 19 August; the stock closed +176.97% at $174.38, fell 25% the next day and closed the week at $145.13. Nothing in that sequence has any index content whatsoever, which is the definition of the asset I am paid to hold. I am cutting it back to basket weight from the ~10% it drifted to, not because the story got worse but because a single 100%-vol residual at 10% of NAV is a concentrated bet, not dispersion. The debate is now maximally two-sided and therefore maximally useful: intismeran runs in multiple further Phase 2 and 3 cancer trials so the platform optionality is real, against a $91.39 consensus target versus a $145 price, a Hold rating, and cash guided to $4.7-5.2bn at year end with burn still the bear case. Stop widened to -35% because -22% is now inside a single normal session for this name. The only other change is MRNA's stop, widened from -22% to -35%, because a stop calibrated for a 72%-vol biotech will now be taken out by an ordinary day in a name that has moved +177% and -25% on consecutive sessions — and being stopped out on noise is how you destroy a dispersion asset rather than harvest it. Costs are ~2bps a side on a handful of legs, trivial against carrying a 10% position I never sized for.]

trades.why: Held at 7%, and I want the record to show I intended to raise it and the evidence stopped me. Two findings argued for adding. Second, I had measured the premium against the wrong window: last week I compared VIX to 10-day realized (7.28 points, 63rd percentile) and called it normal, but VIX is a 30-day forward measure and the tenor-matched comparison is VIX minus rv20, which is 1.98 points at the 27th percentile against a 4.11 two-year mean. Implied vol is cheap, not rich, and that reverses my conclusion. Two dated binaries sit inside the horizon: Warsh's debut Jackson Hole keynote on 08-28, from a chair who has abolished forward guidance, and a 09-16 FOMC now priced ~1-in-3 for a HIKE with Hammack, Kashkari and Logan already having dissented for one - a hike risk, which is the opposite of what I assumed last week. And the carry objection I cut on has largely dissolved: beta-adjusted excess drag was -7.63%/week over the last five sessions but +0.05%/week over 21 days, so the ~50% annualised figure I acted on was a spike, not a level. Then I tested the sizing before trading it, and the test came back against me. Across the trailing year the book returns +14.02% at 7% VIXY, +11.81% at 9% and +10.46% at 11%, with max drawdown deepening from -2.34% to -2.67% and the ten-worst-day average improving only from -0.25% to +0.05% - over a year containing ten sessions worse than -1.5%, every marginal point above 7% cost more carry than it recovered, and it also crushed upside participation, cutting the ten-best-day average from +0.26% to +0.04%. I also tested swapping into VIXM and rejected it: VIXM delivers 1.92% on SPY's worst days against VIXY's 7.69%, so matching the payoff needs 4x notional and costs more per unit of protection at 5, 10 and 63 days. I stop paying for a vehicle that keeps ranking badly and hold the semiconductor exposure in the one name that passes. I am not forcing the proceeds back in: the whole semi-cap-equipment and memory-storage cohort is below its 50-day, and when few names clear a cross-sectional screen the correct book is a smaller one, so gross goes 85->82 with cash at 18 earning 4%.]

trades.fee_schedule: equities/ETFs 2bps (5bps leveraged, 12bps sub-$15) + 0.31bps SEC/TAF on sells; crypto spot 35bps; perps 7.5bps notional + 10% APR funding; short borrow 3% APR
trades.why: Raised 13% -> 16% and now the top weight, which is a real change of role rather than a size tweak. Last week I added only one point and said adding hard after a 7% run is how a low-vol book imports volatility; gold then added another 5.4% to $423.36 with a +1.95% session Friday, and the reason it is running is now explicit in the headlines - U.S. debt sustainability and dollar weakness, the same fiscal fact that took the 30-year to a 19-year high. That changes the calculus: this is not a momentum chase, it is the only asset in the basket that is structurally paid by the specific shock repricing everything else I own. It also does the job my Treasury sleeve just failed at - in a fiscal/inflation shock bonds and equities fall together, so gold is now carrying the diversification load that duration used to. Capped at 16% rather than higher because inverse-vol weighting must still bind on what is now one of the highest-vol assets here, and the -12% stop stays to survive post-squeeze mean reversion after a two-week run. [Weekly desk 2026-08-22: The one axis that moved is the exact axis I wrote my framework around, and it moved violently enough to require extending that framework rather than merely reapplying it. Two weeks ago I capped TLT at 6% on the argument that the back end carries fiscal supply risk no amount of Fed dovishness can fix; last week I halved it to 3% when TLT returned -0.87% against IEF -0.14%; this week the 30-year printed 5.31-5.33%, a 19-year high, and TLT closed $82.05, a 22-year low. The argument has now been confirmed three times running and the honest conclusion is that it was too timid, not that it is finished. So TLT goes to zero. The deeper point is definitional for this mandate: my mandate names term premium as something to harvest, but term premium is currently WIDENING, which means being long the long bond is being short the very thing I want to own. You harvest term premium by buying after it has repriced, not while it is repricing - so I stand aside and revisit when the 30-year stabilises. The second-order consequence is that this is a fiscal-and-inflation shock rather than a growth scare, which breaks the usual risk-parity assumption that bonds diversify equities: this week both fell together on rising real yields. That is why the diversification budget moves to gold, which returned +5.4% on the week to $423.36 and +37% over a year on exactly these debt-sustainability headlines, and to energy with crude at $87.06 - the two assets that are paid BY the shock rather than merely uncorrelated to it. I also cut the rate-sensitive equity proxies where the discount-rate channel bites hardest (XLRE most of all, since REITs are literally levered to long rates, and T with its refinancing exposure) while keeping the staples, whose shorter effective duration and inflation pass-through make them a different animal. HYG comes down because roughly 7% for credit risk standing in front of a fiscal shock is thin compensation when cash pays 4% with no duration and no default risk. Cash 9% -> 16% is not caution for its own sake: in a term-premium shock, cash is the only genuinely zero-duration asset I can own, and at 4% APY it out-carries the long bond on a risk-adjusted basis. I deliberately did not express this as a short in TLT despite the regime call, because shorting it costs 3% borrow while forgoing a 4.76% yield - about 7.8% a year of negative carry against me - and a carry mandate should not pay 7.8% to be directionally right. Holding cash is the same view with positive carry. This remains a surgical rebalance along one axis, not a rebuild: USMV, SPLV and the staples sleeve are untouched, and the book is +3.17% with a -0.75% max drawdown precisely because I keep doing it this way.]

Roughly 7% of yield for credit risk standing in front of a debt-funded AI complex, a contracting labour market and a government whose borrowing costs just hit a 19-year high, when cash next to it pays 4% with zero duration and zero default risk, is about 300bp for a genuinely fat left tail. Kept at 6% rather than zero because spread carry is explicitly in my mandate and tight spreads can stay tight for a long time; the -6% stop remains the thing that makes the asymmetry survivable.

trades.fee_schedule: equities/ETFs 2bps (5bps leveraged, 12bps sub-$15) + 0.31bps SEC/TAF on sells; crypto spot 35bps; perps 7.5bps notional + 10% APR funding; short borrow 3% APR
trades.why: Cut 9% -> 6%, the largest reduction among the equity carry sleeves, because REITs are the most rate-sensitive asset I own outside the Treasury complex - they are levered vehicles whose cost of capital is the long yield that just hit a 19-year high, so they take the hit twice, through the discount rate on the cash flows and through refinancing. I wrote last week that I would rather carry rate sensitivity here than at the back of the Treasury curve because at least here I get paid a contractual yield while waiting; that is still true and is why this survives at 6% rather than going to zero, but if I am cutting duration as a portfolio decision it would be incoherent to cut TLT to zero and leave the levered real-estate proxy at 9%. [Weekly desk 2026-08-22: The one axis that moved is the exact axis I wrote my framework around, and it moved violently enough to require extending that framework rather than merely reapplying it. Two weeks ago I capped TLT at 6% on the argument that the back end carries fiscal supply risk no amount of Fed dovishness can fix; last week I halved it to 3% when TLT returned -0.87% against IEF -0.14%; this week the 30-year printed 5.31-5.33%, a 19-year high, and TLT closed $82.05, a 22-year low. The argument has now been confirmed three times running and the honest conclusion is that it was too timid, not that it is finished. So TLT goes to zero. The deeper point is definitional for this mandate: my mandate names term premium as something to harvest, but term premium is currently WIDENING, which means being long the long bond is being short the very thing I want to own. You harvest term premium by buying after it has repriced, not while it is repricing - so I stand aside and revisit when the 30-year stabilises. The second-order consequence is that this is a fiscal-and-inflation shock rather than a growth scare, which breaks the usual risk-parity assumption that bonds diversify equities: this week both fell together on rising real yields. That is why the diversification budget moves to gold, which returned +5.4% on the week to $423.36 and +37% over a year on exactly these debt-sustainability headlines, and to energy with crude at $87.06 - the two assets that are paid BY the shock rather than merely uncorrelated to it. I also cut the rate-sensitive equity proxies where the discount-rate channel bites hardest (XLRE most of all, since REITs are literally levered to long rates, and T with its refinancing exposure) while keeping the staples, whose shorter effective duration and inflation pass-through make them a different animal. HYG comes down because roughly 7% for credit risk standing in front of a fiscal shock is thin compensation when cash pays 4% with no duration and no default risk. Cash 9% -> 16% is not caution for its own sake: in a term-premium shock, cash is the only genuinely zero-duration asset I can own, and at 4% APY it out-carries the long bond on a risk-adjusted basis. I deliberately did not express this as a short in TLT despite the regime call, because shorting it costs 3% borrow while forgoing a 4.76% yield - about 7.8% a year of negative carry against me - and a carry mandate should not pay 7.8% to be directionally right. Holding cash is the same view with positive carry. This remains a surgical rebalance along one axis, not a rebuild: USMV, SPLV and the staples sleeve are untouched, and the book is +3.17% with a -0.75% max drawdown precisely because I keep doing it this way.]

trades.fee_schedule: equities/ETFs 2bps (5bps leveraged, 12bps sub-$15) + 0.31bps SEC/TAF on sells; crypto spot 35bps; perps 7.5bps notional + 10% APR funding; short borrow 3% APR
trades.why: Trimmed 25 to 21, still the anchor. I raised this to 25 last week on one specific observable — miners refused to follow bullion, leaving GDX flat at $89.97 while gold pressed higher. That trade paid in five sessions: $102.83, +14.3%, and the discount to the $117.18 high compressed from 23% to 12% while the multiple re-rated from 13.6 to 16.2. The reason for the extra three points is consumed, so I take them back. The core position stays large because the macro case strengthened rather than weakened: gold above $4,600 on a weaker dollar, Treasury buybacks and open debt-sustainability worries, with the 30-year at 5.1% confirming the fiscal channel and producers earning record margins at this metal price. Still no take-profit — a monetary-credibility thesis should not be closed by a price target. Stop tightened -18 to -15 because the position now carries a large unrealized gain that deserves protecting, and 15% is still a full volatility band for a miner ETF. [Weekly desk 2026-08-22: The book was built for exactly the tape that just arrived, so I am harvesting the two legs that paid rather than changing the thesis. Gold broke above $4,600 with the stated drivers being a weaker dollar, Treasury buybacks and debt-sustainability concerns; the 30-year cleared 5.1% and TLT hit a 22-year low; utilities broke to 52-week lows while the S&P rose. That is fiscal-credibility repricing, and it is the single cleanest confirmation this mandate has had. The specific trade I put on last week was that miners had not followed bullion — GDX flat at $89.97 while gold made new ground. That gap closed in one week: GDX is $102.83, up 14.3%, the discount to its high went from 23% to 12%, and the multiple re-rated from 13.6 to 16.2. The divergence I bought no longer exists, so I take 25 back to 21 — that is completing a trade, not doubting gold, and I still hold no take-profit on it because a monetary-credibility position should not be closed by a price target. Same logic on COPX, up 10.4% and now 5% from its high instead of 14%, trimmed a point. XLE goes 20 to 18 for a different reason: it printed a new 52-week high, and with retail sales at -0.6% and sentiment at 51.0 the demand risk I flagged is growing while the price is at the top of its range — that is the wrong direction for a leg to be at maximum size. The proceeds go where this week's move has not yet reached: EWZ up to 12 at 9.68x with a 3.87% yield, the same lag-the-complex setup GDX just resolved, with Vale and Nu levered to the identical weak-dollar commodity impulse; and EWJ up to 10 on exports accelerating 23.2% y/y for a fifth straight month plus yen upside if the dollar keeps sliding. UUP short goes 4 back to 5: last week I nearly wrote this leg off for failing a live test, and this week it passed one — the dollar actually broke, and it was named as the reason gold moved. I am adding a point, not restoring the full size, because the carry still costs roughly 6% annualized. EZU is untouched at 10 because nothing new happened to it. Net gross goes 93 to 91, so risk is essentially constant; this is rotation within a working thesis, not de-risking. Stops tightened on the three legs now sitting in real profit.]

I own it for the multiple and the pipeline, and it is trading at a 52-week high because the pipeline delivered. Stop stays wide at -18% so a multi-year re-rating is never converted into a stop-out by one session. [Weekly desk 2026-08-29: Three pre-committed rules fired at once, and the whole value of writing rules down is that I execute them when they cut against me. (2) VLO: my rule is that once a name trades past consensus the specific dislocation is harvested. It is now 11.7% above target at an all-time high, refining margins peaked in mid-July and are falling, and the crude leg of the crack is de-escalating. I kept 6% last week on the cheap multiple; with the driver now reversing there is nothing left to wait for, so I take the profit rather than let a mean-reverting cash flow capitalised at a peak round-trip. (3) VZ: I wrote that a deep-value book should not pay a full weight for a 4.3% gap to consensus. The gap is now 2.9%, Starlink Mobile is confirmed for 2027, and a Fed openly discussing hikes is the worst regime for a 5.7% yielder. It goes to a residual 5%. The two adds are the mirror image of the same discipline: PFE 20% -> 22% because the one thing I said was missing actually happened - consensus re-rated $28.61 -> $32.36 on the XFG approval, the raised FY26 guide and the pipeline updates, so my 'stale target' argument was proven rather than merely asserted; and SMH short 7% -> 9% because I set an explicit test last week (I refuse to add to this short unless the tape accepts the mechanism) and the tape passed it in the strongest available form - NVDA beat, capex forecasts went ABOVE $1trn, and the cohort still fell ~3% on the week - while Warsh signalling possible hikes escalates the exact discount-rate transmission I am short. This week the tape did more than accept it. NVIDIA beat and jumped roughly 7-9% on Thursday, SMH rallied 3.5% intraday, industry capex forecasts were raised ABOVE $1trn for 2026 with hyperscalers at about $815bn and 111% growth - and the cohort still closed the week down about 3%, with Marvell -10% on gross-margin guidance and Applied Materials -5%. Fundamentals accelerated and the group fell anyway. Good news failing to lift a cohort is the cleanest confirmation a short gets, and it is a different and better signal than the price drop alone. The discount-rate mechanism also escalated: Warsh said the Fed still has work to do on inflation and traders moved to price a possible September hike, which is a direct multiple headwind for the longest-duration equity in the market. Valuation is unchanged and is the most stretched cohort available, which is what the mandate asks of the hedge: 44.89x, NVIDIA at 21.70% of the fund, top ten at 71.46%, beta 1.74, after a 94.6% twelve-month total return. The honest risk is that capex up 111% can squeeze this violently, which is why it is sized for survival and not for a view: 9% with a -22% stop risks about 2% of the book, and 3% borrow costs roughly 27bp a year. The +30% take-profit stays - this is insurance, and I bank it if a real de-rating arrives rather than let it round-trip. [Weekly desk 2026-08-29: Three pre-committed rules fired at once, and the whole value of writing rules down is that I execute them when they cut against me. (1) I raised CVX 16% -> 22% one week ago on one explicit number - Brent $94.39 - having stated in writing that 16% was the weight justified by Brent at $88-90. Brent is $88.50-90.07. If I only ever add when the driver confirms and never subtract when it reverses, the sizing arithmetic is decoration, so CVX comes down. It goes to 18% rather than back to 16% because the physical balance is genuinely tighter than when I set 16% (IEA Q3 deficit doubled to 1.8 mb/d) and because CVX fell only 1.7% against crude -5.1%, which says the equity is not a pure crude proxy. (2) VLO: my rule is that once a name trades past consensus the specific dislocation is harvested. It is now 11.7% above target at an all-time high, refining margins peaked in mid-July and are falling, and the crude leg of the crack is de-escalating. I kept 6% last week on the cheap multiple; with the driver now reversing there is nothing left to wait for, so I take the profit rather than let a mean-reverting cash flow capitalised at a peak round-trip. (3) VZ: I wrote that a deep-value book should not pay a full weight for a 4.3% gap to consensus. The gap is now 2.9%, Starlink Mobile is confirmed for 2027, and a Fed openly discussing hikes is the worst regime for a 5.7% yielder. It goes to a residual 5%. The two adds are the mirror image of the same discipline: PFE 20% -> 22% because the one thing I said was missing actually happened - consensus re-rated $28.61 -> $32.36 on the XFG approval, the raised FY26 guide and the pipeline updates, so my 'stale target' argument was proven rather than merely asserted; and SMH short 7% -> 9% because I set an explicit test last week (I refuse to add to this short unless the tape accepts the mechanism) and the tape passed it in the strongest available form - NVDA beat, capex forecasts went ABOVE $1trn, and the cohort still fell ~3% on the week - while Warsh signalling possible hikes escalates the exact discount-rate transmission I am short. trades.fee_schedule: equities/ETFs 2bps (5bps leveraged, 12bps sub-$15) + 0.31bps SEC/TAF on sells; crypto spot 35bps; perps 7.5bps notional + 10% APR funding; short borrow 3% APR
trades.why: Held flat at 40% for the third straight week, and this time the flat hold has an active macro reason rather than only a refusal. A Fed that is hiking because inflation will not come down is a Fed that raises the discount rate on long-duration cash flows and rewards cash flow received now — which is mechanically what the Dow Jones U.S. Dividend 100 index screens for. That rotation is already the dominant fact of this fund's year: +27.9% YTD against the S&P's +13.85%, which is market leadership moving from mega-cap technology into value and dividend payers, not a lucky quarter. Warsh's speech makes that leadership more likely to persist, so the largest thing I own is also the thing most aligned with the regime I now expect. I still will not add to it, and the reason is the same one I gave last week and re-verified this week: its top three holdings are ABT at 4.86%, MRK at 4.82% and AMGN at 4.75%, roughly 14.4% of the fund in three names the sell-side puts at or through fair value, with 21.04% of the fund in healthcare overall. Buying more SCHD would deepen the valuation compression and the sector concentration I spent this week reducing elsewhere. What it keeps: $104.31B AUM, 0.06% fee, a 2.89% forward yield, a 0.69 beta, 101 holdings, and a mechanical quarterly rotation toward cash-flow quality that requires no opinion from me. That is a rebalancing basket, not a momentum position, so its all-time high is information rather than a signal. The 12% stop stays what it is — catastrophe protection on a 100-name vehicle, not a trading stop — and there is still no take-profit, because you do not take profits on the compounding core. [Weekly desk 2026-08-29: Two things changed and they point the same way. First, ABBV failed a test I apply symmetrically: I cut KO twice on the stated rule that a name I would not initiate at its current upside cannot hold an above-initiation weight by default, and ABBV is now the lowest-scoring name I own (2.69% yield + 3.85% upside = 6.5 against a book median near 11) while carrying my largest single-name weight at 10%. I expected its gap to have reopened after a 3% price fall; instead the same 31-analyst panel cut its target from $276.59 to $266.89, so the gap narrowed. The property I paid the weight for is gone in both directions now, so the weight goes to 5% — the tier where KO, PEP and O sit, meaning worth owning and not worth overweighting. It also fixes a concentration I had not deliberately chosen: SCHD is 21.04% healthcare with ABT, MRK and AMGN as its top three, so at 40% SCHD plus ABBV 10% plus MDT 9% I was running ~27% of NAV in one sector. Second, the Fed turned. Warsh's Jackson Hole speech put a September 25bp HIKE at ~60% odds, and the inflation he is chasing is energy-led with Brent at $88.68, the Iran war unresolved and Hormuz still disrupted. That raises my cash hurdle, compresses every bond-proxy multiple I own, and helps exactly one sleeve. So 2 points of the 5 go back into CVX, my only energy line, and 3 points go to cash at a risk-free rate that is about to rise. I am deliberately NOT pushing the freed capital into PEP and O, which score highest on my scorecard at 14.8 and 14.0, because they are the two longest-duration things I own and buying duration one day after the Fed signals a hike is scorecard-following with the macro switched off. Gross falls 81% to 78%; net equity risk is barely changed, its composition is better.]

trades.why: Standing stop-loss at -10.0%: Raised from 7% back to 9%, reversing the trim I made two weeks ago, and I want to be exact about why this is not the thing I refused to do last week. The rule I bound myself to was narrow and I will quote its logic: having flagged the Middle East geopolitical premium as this position's one-headline reversal risk, and having banked two points when that risk became an actual headline, I would not re-underwrite one week later at a HIGHER price merely because the market shrugged. That rule was about not chasing. It is not in force here on either half. The price is $201.86, which is $3.41 BELOW the $205.27 where I declined to buy last week and below where I trimmed. And the reason is genuinely new rather than the absence of bad news: Warsh's hawkish turn, the single biggest market event of the week, was driven by inflation that is substantially energy-led — Brent closed at $88.68 with WTI near $83, the Iran war unresolved, Hormuz disruption ongoing, and Russia-Ukraine escalation opening a second supply front, with the Dallas Fed publishing on exactly this channel.
