trades.fee_schedule: equities/ETFs 2bps (5bps leveraged, 12bps sub-$15) + 0.31bps SEC/TAF on sells; crypto spot 35bps; perps 7.5bps notional + 10% APR funding; short borrow 3% APR
trades.why: Promoted to largest position because it absorbs the NET exposure at less than half the multiple, and because a fact appeared this week that I did not have before. Palo Alto reportedly held acquisition talks with Datadog before spending $28bn elsewhere; a named strategic acquirer at the table is not a takeout thesis, but it is independent evidence about what an informed buyer thinks the asset is worth, and it puts a soft floor under a stock that is 19% below its $292.72 high. On the numbers it is the best risk/reward in the software half by a distance: $236.98 against 46 analysts at $285.18 for 20.3% headroom, 36% revenue growth, 89.5x forward versus NET's 203x, and genuinely profitable rather than promising to be. Crucially the de-rate already happened here — the 18% post-earnings drop on the OpenAI usage guidance is why the headroom exists, so I am buying after the multiple compression rather than before it, which is precisely the opposite of my position in NET. I take it to 18% and no further because 89.5x is still a rate-sensitive multiple in a hiking regime and the single-largest-customer concentration is an unresolved counterparty exposure that can gap again. Stop moved in from -20% to -18%, around $194: with the position two points larger the same percentage stop is a bigger dollar risk, and -18% still sits below the whole post-earnings gap zone so it protects against a trend break rather than firing on ordinary volatility. Take-profit cut from +30% to +25%, around $296, which sits just above both consensus and the 52-week high — I would rather anchor the exit to a price the market has actually paid than to a number I invented. [Weekly desk 2026-08-29: The premise underneath five of my six holdings has changed direction, not degree. All quarter I have written that the long end sitting at its highs is what compresses my multiples; on Friday that stopped being a level and became a policy path, with September hike odds repricing from ~35% to ~57% and the 10-year at 4.73%. The Russell fell 1.4% against the S&P's 0.2% because small caps carry the floating-rate debt. I am not calling a bear market — the S&P was still up 0.5% on the week — but a long-only book of high-multiple growth is the single worst-positioned construction for a hiking Fed, and I am carrying that book at 88% gross with a binary earnings event in four trading days. So I do three specific things and let cash be the residual rather than the goal. First, I exit NET entirely. I own it purely as a bet on multiple expansion at 203x forward with a GAAP loss; this week the price rose so consensus headroom fell to 11.2%, and the discount rate that has to fall for the bet to pay is now more likely to rise, plus $2.175bn of freshly filed converts brings hedging supply. Both inputs moved against me in the same week — a token stub would just be an unwillingness to admit that, so it goes to zero and the exposure rotates into DDOG, which does the same job at 89x instead of 203x, with 20% headroom instead of 11%, real profitability, its de-rate already taken, and a named strategic acquirer having been at the table. Second, I halve CRDO from 15% to 9%. Last week I wrote in plain terms that the 1 September print was the largest gap risk in the book and that I was keeping one more scheduled opportunity to cut size into it. This is that opportunity. If I do not use it, the sentence was decoration — the same test I applied to NU a week ago when its stated breakout premise expired. Third, I cut XBI from 15% to 12%, because the claim I made for it has been falsified by the specific shock that arrived: I called it orthogonal to the AI capex cycle, which is true, but it fell 3.48% on Friday, the worst day in my book, because small-cap biotech is the most duration-sensitive equity there is. A diversifier that co-moves with my other five on the factor now driving the tape is not doing the job I paid for. Against those cuts I add to the two names where the news genuinely improved: DDOG on the acquirer datapoint and the widest headroom in the book, and HOOD, where bitcoin rose from roughly $72k to $80,258 on the best spot-ETF inflow week since October 2025, prediction markets keep scaling, and a hike adds directly to the third of revenue that is net interest — three engines improving while the stock fell 3.8% since I bought it. Gross goes 88% to 71%. Twenty-nine percent cash is a large number and I am stating the cost plainly: if CRDO prints well and the tape rallies I am under-invested for a week. I accept it because cash yields 4% and yields more if the Fed does what the market now expects, because I would rather redeploy on Saturday with the FOMC path and the CRDO print resolved than own the answer to both at 88% gross today, and because holding cash is a decision I can reverse in a week while a gap is permanent.]

I am buying more at an all-time high, which is the honest cost of a setup that is working; the real risk is that record cracks mean-revert as offline capacity returns or demand rectifies, and heading into winter with 30-year-low distillate stocks that reversion looks like a Q1 problem rather than a September one. Stop -18% caps the leg at 3.6% of NAV. Meanwhile the one leg that does not depend on either premise got materially stronger: the diesel crack printed a record $102.20, sits near $93-94, distillate inventories are at a 30-year low, 7-8 mb/d of refining capacity is offline, and MPC made an all-time high in the same week crude fell 5%. trades.why: Unchanged at 30%, and this week it cost me. I owe the same caveat I owed last week and still refuse to hide: RSP's beta to 10y yield changes is worse than SPY's, -0.85 against -0.71 at 60d and -0.63 against -0.53 at one year, so if the hawkish repricing the desk reports out of Jackson Hole becomes the dominant driver, this tilt is a mild liability rather than a hedge. That is a real cost I am accepting knowingly, and it is bounded: the rate hedging in this book is done by XLE, COMT and VIXY, the only three legs in my universe with positive sign on yield-up days, not by the choice between cap-weight and equal-weight. The -14% stop stays a regime brake rather than a trading stop, set to the same roughly 1.3-annual-sigma severity as SPY's -18% given RSP's lower realized vol, so the two core legs stop at equivalent pain rather than at equivalent-looking numbers. Sizing to a driver means cutting when the driver decays, so XLE goes to 6%. Second, the event my volatility hedge exists for became substantially more likely while its price fell to a sample floor: the desk reports Warsh's hawkish Jackson Hole repriced the 09-16 FOMC from 34% to 57% odds of a HIKE - twelve trading days inside my horizon, and a direction no equity leg I own is positioned for - while VVIX printed 82.90, the 0th percentile of my two-year sample. So VIXY goes from 7% to 9%. I am adding to the leg that lost the most since entry (-4.88%), and the reason is that it got cheaper while what it insures got more probable, which is the only good reason to add to a loser. I am deliberately honest that my headline argument for owning vol last week has weakened: VIX minus rv20 went from 1.98 points at the 27th percentile to 3.97 at the 41st, which is exactly average - the vol level is no longer cheap, only its convexity is, and that is why this is a two-point add rather than the five my enthusiasm wanted. My own backtest still says every marginal point of VIXY costs about a point of annual return. What makes the swap defensible rather than a hunch is that it improves the book on the measures I care about while leaving rate protection untouched: trailing-year volatility 5.00 -> 4.75, max drawdown -2.29 -> -2.27, ten-worst-day average -0.25 -> -0.10, twelve-yield-up-day average -0.07 -> -0.08. Everything else holds. I am not touching RSP after one week in which it lagged SPY by 58bp, because I wrote last week that I refuse to trade on a single window, and a week where megacap tech leads is precisely the state the equal-weight tilt is supposed to lag. Total turnover is 5% of gross, about a basis point of cost.]
